newsitem.title: KAZAKHSTAN: Delhi crash involves controversial Kazakh airline.
newsitem.headline: Delhi crash involves controversial Kazakh airline.

text.p: The Kazakh cargo plane which collided in mid-air on Tuesday with a Saudi jumbo jet near Delhi is said to belong to an airline with huge debts and a controversial safety record.
There was no clue by early Wednesday of what caused the world's worst mid-air catastrophe, which may have claimed some 350 lives. Any number of factors may have contributed.
It is the latest of many aircraft from the economically depressed former Soviet Union to meet disaster in recent years.

The state airline which Kazakh and Indian officials said owned the doomed Ilyushin Il-76TD freighter has been dogged by financial problems and was formally closed down in August after being criticised by the government for falling safety standards.

The Kazakh government assumed control of its share of Aeroflot under the name Kazakhstan National Airways. Air transport officials in Almaty and Delhi identified this company, locally known as KazAir, as the owner of the doomed Delhi jet.
It was chartered by a firm in the Kyrgyz capital Bishkek and took off from Chimkent in southern Kazakhstan for Delhi with 10 crew and 28 passengers, many of them Kyrgyz nationals.

Formally, Kazakhstan National Airways, one of hundreds of "babyflots" spawned by the break-up of Aeroflot as the Soviet Union broke up in 1991, was closed down in August after running up $149 million in debts.
An official inquiry found its planes were badly serviced and the fleet could cease to meet international safety norms.
One of the airline's Tupolev Tu-154 passenger jets caught fire on take-off at Kiev in July. No one was hurt.
An international aviation insurance expert told Reuters recently that some airlines from Kazakhstan had difficulty obtaining international insurance cover because of safety fears.
The Almaty government formally set up a new national airline, Air Kazakhstan, to take over KazAir's operations.
Cash shortages and cut-throat competition have been blamed for falling airline safety standards across Moscow's old empire.
Aircraft manufacturers defend their products and blame poor maintenance and overstretched crews for problems.
Ilyushin 76s, four-engined craft common in the former Soviet cargo fleet and now chartered extensively by cost-conscious foreign operators, have suffered a number of recent accidents.
One owned by a private Russian firm crashed at Belgrade in August as the pilot attempted an emergency landing. All 10 crew aboard were killed.
In June, a Ukrainian Il-76 crashed on take-off at Kinshasa in Zaire, again killing the 10-man crew. In April, 12 died when an Il-76 came down on the far eastern Kamchatka peninsula.

Kinshasa was the site of one of the world's worst air crashes when, in January this year, a Russian Antonov An-32 ploughed into a crowded marketplace shortly after take-off. Some 350 were killed. Two Russian pilots are in a Zairean jail.
A Russian An-124 freighter came down on houses last month near Turin, killing two of the crew and two Italian villagers.
In general, there has been much greater loss of life involving passenger aircraft.
More than 140 people, mostly Ukrainian coalminers and their families, died when a Russian Tupolev Tu-154 slammed into a mountain on Norway's Arctic island of Spitsbergen in August.
The U.S. Federal Aviation Authority said last December after the crash of a Tu-154 in the Far East that Russian airlines were "minimally meeting requirements" for international air safety.
The most notorious crash of recent years was in March 1994, when 70 people died after an Aeroflot pilot allowed his teenage son to send an Airbus A310 crashing into the Siberian taiga.
